implementation_notes: C++11 absorbed the pattern into the language: a thread_local variable has thread storage duration, so there is a distinct object per thread and the declared name refers to the current thread's entity; block-scope thread_local implies static and is initialised on the first pass through the declaration; and objects with thread storage duration are destroyed at thread exit (the standard's [basic.stc.thread]). The key/collection/proxy structure of the classic pattern is replaced by the declaration itself. Because the declaration is the access point, the object is directly addressable and needs no proxy or smart pointer; the classic key-based form stays justified only for pre-C++11 toolchains or when a per-thread object must be created and replaced at runtime.
pitfalls: References or pointers to thread_local objects must not escape their thread: another thread would touch storage that belongs to a different object, and the object is destroyed when its own thread exits.
Destruction order between thread_local objects and POSIX thread-specific data is platform-specific (glibc: thread_locals first), so a TSD destructor must not use a thread_local object.
A thread_local in a dynamically loaded module can use the dynamic TLS model with slower access; a hot-path guarantee taken from the static model may not hold after dlopen().
Values are per thread, not per task: in a thread pool they survive across work items and must be reset explicitly, and coroutines resumed on a shared executor thread share one instance.

variants.name: boost::thread_specific_ptr (portable, pre-C++11)
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.Thread's thread_specific_ptr is the portable realization for C++03 toolchains and for code that must create and re-bind a per-thread object at runtime: the instance is a smart pointer that uses its own address as the key (so no lock-protected key allocation is needed), get()/reset()/release() manage the calling thread's pointer, and the object is deleted or handed to a supplied cleanup routine when the thread exits. Choose it when the toolchain predates thread_local, when the object must be replaced during the thread's life, or when a cleanup routine other than delete is required; prefer the keyword wherever it is available, because the Boost key costs an associative-container lookup per access.
pitfalls: On some platforms cleanup is performed only for threads started through Boost; a thread created with the native API leaks its thread-specific object unless Boost.on_thread_exit() is called from it.
The destructor requires the other threads' values to be null already, and no running thread may touch the instance afterwards - keep such objects alive for the process lifetime.
Access goes through an associative container keyed by the pointer's address, which is measurably slower than the native thread_local keyword.

variants.name: ACE_TSS smart-pointer proxy (POSA2 classic)
variants.implementation_notes: ACE ships the pattern in its canonical POSA2 shape: ACE_TSS<TYPE> is the TS Object Proxy - an object that is logically global while the TYPE instance is physically per thread - and operator->() hides both the key and the collection (the ACE documentation states that all threads access a single ACE_TSS instance to obtain a pointer to a thread-specific copy, and that instances are deleted when the ACE_TSS object is destroyed or the thread exits). Choose it inside an ACE code base, where its thread-management and service-configurator layers are already the concurrency substrate, or when studying the pattern in its documented form; new code should use thread_local or Boost instead.
pitfalls: Destroying the ACE_TSS instance deletes every thread's copy, so a stack-allocated proxy around long-lived threads is a use-after-free.
The ACE build is C++03-era and brings its own locking and thread-management layer; mixing it with C++11 thread_local splits the concurrency model inside one code base.
